title: Kunti Asks Only for Remembrance
subtitle: A queen's farewell hymn as Krishna turns toward Dwaraka
story:
The brahma weapon of Ashvatthama had been spent that night and turned back, and the sons of Pandu stood alive in the wreckage of it. Krishna had stayed only long enough to see them safe. Now he was turning toward Dwaraka, his own city, and Kunti — who had thanked him in her heart through a lifetime of dangers — knew she might not see him again like this, with the world grown quiet. She had watched him save her sons so many times that the court had lost count of the rescues.

She came forward as he turned to depart, and she spoke. The mother of kings, Yudhishthira and his brothers standing silent behind her, addressed him in the hearing of the whole court; and what poured out of her was not a plea but a hymn.

She bowed to the primal Person, veiled by his own play, unknowable to the ignorant, imperishable; the goal of the pure-hearted sages. She bowed to Krishna, son of Vasudeva, son of Devaki, lotus-navelled, garlanded with lotuses. She remembered his mother shut away for years in Kamsa's prison, given over to sorrow — and freed at last. Then she remembered herself. Poison had come to her sons, and the great fire, and the cruel assembly of the dice hall, and the long hardships of forest exile, and the weapons of the mightiest warriors of the age. From all of these, again and again, he had freed her and her children.

And then Kunti said the thing that made the court go still. "May those dangers remain with me forever, teacher of the world," she said, "for it was in danger that I saw you. A man puffed up by birth, by wealth, by learning, by beauty, does not see you at all." She bowed again — to him who is the wealth of those who own nothing, who stands beyond the pull of the world's moods. "I consider you Time itself," she said, "the lord without beginning and without end. No one can read your intention, for you move among us in the guise of a man. Your birth, your deeds — though you are unborn and do nothing. Even the rope with which a gopi of Vrindavan bound you as a child, when you had misbehaved, your eyes blurred with tears and running collyrium — even that was your play."

People argued about why he had come at all, she said. Some held that the unborn one took birth to give glory to the virtuous. Others said Vasudeva had prayed for him, and he came to Devaki. Others said he came to lift the earth's burden, as a boat is lowered onto a drowning sea. Whatever the truth — and the wise could not agree — the troubled of this world heard of his deeds and sang them, chanted them, remembered them, and took joy in them.

Then the hymn found its wound. "Will you abandon us today, lord?" she asked. "Will you leave your friends, your servants? What are we, Pandavas and Yadavas alike, without you, but name and form? This land will not shine as it shines now, bearer of the mace, once you are gone." And she named him as the verses name him — Shri Krishna, friend of Arjuna, bull of the Vrishnis, whose valor has no end.

The court was silent. And Kunti, who in all those years had asked nothing for herself — no kingdom, no wealth, no safety — asked the one thing she wanted. "May my mind be fixed on you alone, lord of Madhu," she said. "Again and again, on you alone."

Krishna, whose every glory she had praised, smiled gently. "So be it," he answered her. And he turned back toward the city.
reflection: Kunti's hymn is one of the strangest farewells in the tradition: she does not ask Krishna to stay, only that her remembrance of him stay. Her prayer that dangers might remain forever is not a love of suffering but a confession that it was in danger that she knew him most clearly — gratitude so complete that it can thank even misfortune.
next_story_tease: Krishna granted her prayer, but he would not leave the city that day — there were months of leave-taking still ahead.
hero_scene: Queen Kunti, hands folded in salutation, stands before Krishna in the morning light of Hastinapura as he turns toward his chariot; the Pandava court silent behind her, and Krishna smiling gently as he answers her hymn.
